newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FOCUS-Sri Lanka president may be mulling general election. [CORRECTED 11:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Sri Lanka president may be mulling general election. [CORRECTED 11:00 GMT]

text.p: A big win by her ruling coalition in Friday's local-level polls could tempt Sri Lankan President Chandrika Kumaratunga to call general elections ahead of schedule, diplomats and analysts said.

A comfortable victory in the local polls might convince Kumaratunga that the public supports her plan for ending the 13-year war with ethnic Tamil separatists, especially a proposal to grant wide autonomy to minorities, they said on Friday. (Corrects to clarify autonomy intended for minorities).
They noted a mere one-seat majority for Kumaratunga's People's Alliance (PA) coalition was the main obstacle to her peace package being adopted by the 225-member parliament.
General elections are not due until 1999.

"There is a lot of speculation, but it will depend on how much they win by. It will not make much difference if they just scrape through. But if they get a comfortable majority, then parliamentary elections seem to be on," said an Asian diplomat.
"There seems to be a strong chance that general elections may be called if she wins by a big margin," said Paikashotty Sarvanamattu of the Centre for Policy Research, an independent think tank.

Sri Lankans were voting on Friday to elect members to 238 local councils in what was widely seen as the first political test for Kumaratunga's People's Alliance, which won power in 1994, ending 17 years of rule by the main opposition United National Party (UNP).
Jaydeva Uyangoda, an respected social scientist, said the local polls were "like a mid-term referendum on government's performance".
"If PA wins, it will take it as an affirmation of its policies," he added.

Kumaratunga's peace proposal, which requires a new constitution to be written, grants extensive autonomy to the regions and is aimed at ending the war by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) for a separate homeland in the island's north and east.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the war. The LTTE says the number is higher.
The plan also calls for the abolition of the presidency and a return to a British-style parliamentary system.

The devolution package is currently with a select committee and is expected to be presented to parliament before November. If approved by a two-thirds majority, which is difficult without UNP support, it would be placed before the people in a referendum.

The government has also mentioned the possibility of a "non-binding" referendum aimed at gauging public opinion before the new constitution is tabled in parliament. If it gets the green light, Kumaratunga could then be in a position to pressure the UNP into going along with the proposals.
Uyangoda said the government would be better off opting for a non-binding referendum than calling general elections.

"The situation is different than in 1994. Then, the Tamils voted for the PA. They might not go for her this time as they know the chances of this government settling the conflict are not good," he said.
"She has to be sure she will get a fairly good majority," a Western diplomat told Reuters. "If she loses general elections, she might be constrained as president."
But the Asian diplomat said Kumaratunga, who as president serves until her term expires in 2000, might gamble on an election since her position is secure.
